speaker: russell
text: All right, here's what I need to tell you, ma'am. The law in Texas says there's only supposed to be one lawsuit at a time going on concerning the minor children. It also says that whenever people who are married and have children together get a divorce, that the lawsuit about the divorce has to include a lawsuit about the children. Well, if you already have an attorney general's case or some other kind of case where you have child support being ordered, that's a separate lawsuit. So you have to combine them together. Now, the easiest way to do that if the order in the attorney general's case is working out, if it's current, if it doesn't need to be changed, the easiest way is just to get a copy of whatever the final order is in the attorney general's case. And you write on the divorce decree, just a little handwritten, can be a handwritten note that says, and it's for the children, we're going to adopt the order from the attorney general's case. Here's a copy of it. And that's the order of the court in the divorce suit. If there's something that needs to be changed or you want to have, either one of you wants to have change, then those changes can be made. But you've got to do one or the other. OK? The other thing I need to talk to both of you about is the law in Texas presumes that every single thing a married person owns is community property. So it's not a matter of whose name is on a piece of property. It's not a matter of whether the two of you are fighting over a piece of property. Anything that's valuable enough, there might be a lawsuit over it one day. You need to make sure you spell out in the divorce decree who gets it. And either say that it is community property and it's being divided up, or if it's not community property because, for instance, it was inherited or it was owned before the marriage, then say, hey, this is not community property and it's not being divided up. If one of those two things doesn't happen, then the law presumes that I, the judge, forgot to divide that property up and that the two of you still own it together, even though you're divorced. And 20 years from now, either the ex-spouse or their creditors can come back into court and say, wait a minute. We want part of whatever piece of property the divorce decree didn't describe.
